name: CMT X-linked (GJB1/connexin 32)
aliases: X-linked hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy

clinicalPearls: X-linked neuropathy caused by variants in GJB1, which encodes connexin 32, a gap-junction protein expressed at Schwann cell paranodes and Schmidt-Lanterman incisures
Male predominant: hemizygous men are affected more severely and earlier than heterozygous women, who may be mildly affected or asymptomatic
Clinical picture resembles CMT with distal wasting, foot deformity and sensory loss, but onset is often in the second decade
Because there is no male-to-male transmission, an X-linked inheritance pattern is a strong pointer to a GJB1 cause
Nerve conduction velocities are typically intermediate, lying between the markedly slow demyelinating range and the near-normal axonal range, often with a degree of asymmetry
Transient central nervous system episodes with reversible white-matter changes on imaging can occur, sometimes provoked by fever, altitude or exertion
Diagnosis is confirmed by GJB1 sequencing in the appropriate clinical and inheritance context
reference.pathophysiology: GJB1 encodes connexin 32, which forms gap-junction channels that allow rapid radial diffusion of ions and small molecules across the myelin sheath between the Schwann cell body and the adaxonal cytoplasm. Loss of functional channels impairs Schwann cell-axon communication and myelin maintenance, producing a mixed demyelinating and axonal neuropathy. The X-linked pattern explains the greater severity in males, while random X-inactivation accounts for the milder and more variable expression in females. Connexin 32 is also expressed in central oligodendrocytes, which underlies the occasional reversible central white-matter dysfunction seen in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Acquired demyelinating neuropathy with central involvement
Multifocal acquired demyelinating sensory and motor neuropathy
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies typically showing intermediate velocities, sometimes asymmetric
GJB1 sequencing guided by an X-linked family history
Careful pedigree analysis noting absence of male-to-male transmission
Brain MRI when transient central neurological symptoms occur, which may show reversible white-matter signal change
Assessment of female relatives who may harbour milder disease
Exclusion of acquired inflammatory neuropathy where the course is atypical
redFlags: Acute encephalopathic or stroke-like episodes with white-matter change requiring urgent evaluation
Rapid deterioration suggesting a superimposed inflammatory process
Severe early disability in a young male indicating aggressive disease
Bulbar or respiratory involvement, which is atypical and warrants review
reference.prognosis: Affected males usually have slowly progressive disability but commonly remain ambulant, while most female carriers have mild or no symptoms. Transient central episodes typically resolve, and overall life expectancy is normal.
pitfalls: Dismissing a mildly affected mother and missing the X-linked inheritance clue
Misinterpreting intermediate conduction velocities as an acquired neuropathy
Attributing reversible central episodes to stroke and initiating inappropriate treatment
Failing to offer genetic counselling regarding the X-linked recurrence pattern
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No specific therapy for the underlying connexin-32 defect, so physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain strength and function with stretching to prevent contractures are the foundation of care
Ankle-foot orthoses and supportive footwear for foot drop, with orthopaedic surgery for fixed foot deformity
Neuropathic pain managed with agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclics where troublesome
Recognise and reassure over transient central nervous system episodes, advising avoidance of provoking factors such as fever, high altitude and extreme exertion
Avoid neurotoxic drugs such as vincristine that may worsen the neuropathy
Neuromuscular multidisciplinary team involvement including podiatry, orthotics and rehabilitation
Genetic counselling explaining X-linked inheritance and absence of male-to-male transmission, with assessment of potentially affected female relatives
